title: Who Is Jesus?
subtitle: Isa ibn Maryam in Islam and Christ in Christianity — two answers to history's most important question
summary: Islam and Christianity both honor Jesus, his virgin birth, his Messiahship, and his miracles. Their decisive disagreement is whether Jesus is God or God's messenger. The Quran calls him the Messiah and Word from God, yet also God's servant who tells people to worship his Lord and theirs. The Gospels preserve the same pattern of prayer, dependence, and mission. Islam invites people to love Jesus without directing worship away from the one God he worshiped.

sections.title: Jesus the Messiah: Honored, Miraculous, and a Servant of God
sections.body: Islam and Christianity both honor Jesus, his virgin birth, his Messiahship, and his miracles. Their decisive disagreement is whether Jesus is God or God's messenger. The Quran calls him the Messiah and Word from God, yet also God's servant who tells people to worship his Lord and theirs. The Gospels preserve the same pattern of prayer, dependence, and mission. Islam invites people to love Jesus without directing worship away from the one God he worshiped.

sections.title: Introduction: A Question Both Faiths Care About
sections.body:
No conversation between a Muslim and a Christian gets very far before it arrives at Jesus. That is not an accident. For Christians, Jesus is the center of the faith itself. For Muslims, belief in Jesus is not optional either: the Quran names him dozens of times, includes Surah Maryam, a chapter bearing his mother Mary's name, and makes belief in him one of the required articles of faith. A person cannot be a Muslim while rejecting Jesus.

This surprises many readers meeting Islam for the first time. Islam is, in a real sense, a Jesus-affirming religion. It affirms his miraculous virgin birth, his title of Messiah (al-Masih in Arabic — the anointed one promised to the Children of Israel), his miracles, and his honored rank among the greatest messengers God ever sent.

Where the two faiths part ways is on one precise point: is Jesus divine? Christianity's mainstream answer, settled in its creeds, is yes — he is God the Son, fully divine and fully human. Islam's answer is no — he is God's servant and messenger, fully human and nothing less than magnificent in that role.

Because the disagreement is precise, it can be examined honestly. In what follows, every verse of the Quran and the Bible is quoted directly from its source text, so that nothing rests on anyone's memory or paraphrase.

sections.title: The Real Question: Not Whether Jesus Matters, but Who He Is
sections.body:
It helps to clear away what is not in dispute. Islam and Christianity agree that Jesus existed, that he was born of the Virgin Mary without a human father, that he is the Messiah, that he performed genuine miracles, that he taught people to worship God, and that his story is not over — both traditions expect his return before the end of history.

That is a remarkable amount of common ground. The disagreement sits on top of it, and it can be stated in one sentence. Christianity says Jesus is the Creator who entered His creation; Islam says Jesus is the greatest of a long line of human messengers sent by the Creator.

Everything else — the Trinity, the crucifixion as atonement for sin, the meaning of the title 'Son of God' — flows from that single fork in the road.

So the fair way to proceed is to ask three questions in order. What does the Quran say Jesus is? What does the Bible say Jesus is, as mainstream Christianity reads it? And when the two sets of texts are placed side by side, which portrait do they most naturally support? The sections below take those questions one at a time.

sections.title: Jesus in His Jewish and Historical Setting
sections.body:
Jesus lived as a Jew in first-century Judea and Galilee under Roman rule. His religious world centered on the one God of Israel, and Mark records him affirming the Shema: "The Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Mark 12:29).

After Jesus, his followers debated how to describe his status. The New Testament already contains different forms of exalted language, while the precise formulas of Trinity and two natures were defined through later controversies, especially at Nicaea in 325 and Chalcedon in 451. Christians see those councils as clarification; Muslims see them as evidence that Jesus's simple monotheistic message was later recast in philosophical terms.

sections.title: Jesus in the Quran
sections.body:
The Quran introduces Jesus through honor, not rejection. Mary receives the announcement of "a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary" (Quran 3:45). Jesus is born without a human father, speaks as an infant, heals the blind and leper, and raises the dead—always "by God's permission" (Quran 3:49; 5:110).

The same Quran defines his identity. Jesus says, "I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet" (Quran 19:30). Quran 4:171 calls him Messiah, messenger, word, and spirit from God, then warns against saying "Three" because God is one. Quran 5:72 records his call: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."

These titles fit together. "Word" refers to God's creative command, not a second divine person; Quran 3:59 compares Jesus's fatherless creation with Adam's creation. Jesus's miracles prove God's power working through a chosen messenger, not the messenger's independent deity.

sections.title: The Strongest Christian Texts
sections.body:
Christians commonly cite John 1:1, John 8:58, John 20:28, Philippians 2:6-8, Colossians 2:9, and Hebrews 1:3. Read within Nicene theology, these passages support Christ's preexistence and divinity. They should not be ignored or misquoted.

They also need to be read beside Jesus's own words: the Father is "the only true God" (John 17:3), "greater than I" (John 14:28), and "my God and your God" (John 20:17). Jesus prays, obeys, and says he can do nothing by himself (John 5:30). The Islamic reading treats those direct statements as the key to the more exalted language.

sections.title: Jesus in the Bible
sections.body:
The Gospels show Jesus living as a servant of God. He prays before major decisions (Luke 6:12), falls on his face in Gethsemane and submits his will to God's (Matthew 26:39), and identifies the greatest commandment as worship of the one Lord (Mark 12:29-30). Peter calls him "a man attested to you by God" through signs that "God did through him" (Acts 2:22). Paul distinguishes "one God" from "one mediator ... the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5).

Christians interpret these passages through the incarnation: Jesus is fully human as well as divine. Muslims accept their plain prophetic meaning. A man sent, empowered, and heard by God is magnificent—but he is not the God who sent and empowered him.

sections.title: One Messiah, Two Conclusions
sections.body:
Both faiths affirm Jesus as Messiah, born miraculously to Mary, morally pure, and supported by miracles. Christianity goes further and worships him as God the Son. Islam stops where Jesus's own pattern points: he is God's Messiah and servant.

The Islamic portrait does not make Jesus smaller. Prophethood is among the highest honors God gives a human being. It also preserves the distinction found throughout Jesus's prayers: one is the worshiper and the other is the God being worshiped.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
Misconception one: 'Muslims reject Jesus.' The opposite is true. Belief in Jesus as the Messiah and a true messenger of God is a required article of Islamic faith. The Quran mentions Jesus by name far more often than it mentions Muhammad (peace be upon them both), and Muslims traditionally add 'peace be upon him' whenever they say his name. What Islam rejects is not Jesus but his deification.

Misconception two: 'Christians worship three gods.' Mainstream Christian theology explicitly denies this. The doctrine of the Trinity, as Christian scholarship defines it, is that one God exists in three persons — a form of monotheism on its own definition. The Quran's command 'do not say, "Three"' (Quran 4:171) is understood by Muslims as a warning against any formulation that divides God's absolute oneness, however it is labeled; but honest dialogue requires describing the Trinity as Christians actually teach it, not as a crude tritheism.

Misconception three: 'The Quran calls Jesus a "word from God," so it secretly affirms his divinity.' In the Quran's own explanation, Jesus is a 'word' because he came into being by God's creative command — 'He only says to it, "Be," and it is' (Quran 3:47). The title marks the miracle of his conception, not a share in God's essence.

Misconception four: 'Islam denies the virgin birth and the miracles.' It affirms both, emphatically. Jesus' virgin birth (Quran 3:45-47) and his 'clear proofs' — his miracles, performed with God's support (Quran 2:87) — are Quranic doctrine. Notably, Acts 2:22 frames the miracles the same way: works 'which God did by him.'

Misconception five: 'Denying Jesus' divinity means disrespecting him.' In the Islamic view, calling Jesus God's faithful servant is not a demotion; servanthood to God is the highest honor a creature can hold, and Jesus himself is quoted opening his mission with exactly that title: 'Indeed, I am the servant of Allah' (Quran 19:30).

sections.title: Love Jesus and Worship the God He Worshiped
sections.body:
Islam asks Christians to return to the God Jesus called "my God and your God." It accepts every true miracle and honor God gave him while refusing to give a creature the worship due to the Creator.

The Quran's Jesus is coherent from beginning to end: created by God's command, strengthened by God's permission, speaking God's message, saved by God, and returning before the Last Day. He is the Messiah to follow, not the God to worship. Loving Jesus and worshiping God alone are not competing loyalties; in Islam, they belong together.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Jesus in Islam and Christianity
sections.body: Jesus is central to Islam: Messiah, miracle-worker, and mighty messenger. The central question is not whether to honor him, but whether to worship him. His prayers and direct sayings distinguish him from the one God who sent him. The Quran confirms that distinction and invites humanity to follow Jesus in submission to God alone.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe in Jesus?
A: Yes — belief in Jesus is mandatory in Islam. Muslims believe he is the Messiah, born of the Virgin Mary, a mighty messenger of God who performed miracles by God's permission. Rejecting Jesus would place a person outside Islam.

Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus is God or the son of God?
A: No. The Quran teaches that Jesus is God's servant and messenger, fully human, and explicitly states that God is exalted above having a son (Quran 4:171). Islam sees the deification of Jesus as the kind of 'excess in religion' the Quran warns against.

Q: Does Islam accept the virgin birth of Jesus?
A: Yes. The Quran narrates the annunciation to Mary and her astonished question — 'How will I have a child when no man has touched me?' — answered by God's creative command: 'Be,' and it is (Quran 3:47). The virgin birth is a miracle of creation, not proof of divine sonship.

Q: What does 'Messiah' mean in Islam?
A: Al-Masih (the Messiah) is a title of honor the Quran gives uniquely to Jesus, marking him as the anointed one promised to the Children of Israel. The Quran pairs the title with 'son of Mary' and 'messenger of Allah' (Quran 4:171, 5:75), so in Islam it does not imply divinity.

Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus was crucified?
A: Mainstream Islamic teaching holds that Jesus was not killed by crucifixion but that God saved him and raised him to Himself, and that he will return before the end of time.

Q: If both faiths love Jesus, why does the difference matter?
A: Because both faiths agree that who God is — and who may be worshiped — is the most important question a person faces. If Jesus is God, refusing him worship is a grave error; if he is God's human messenger, directing worship to him is exactly the excess the Quran, and arguably Jesus' own recorded words, warn against.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **The Muslim Jesus: Sayings and Stories in Islamic Literature** — Tarif Khalidi. A Cambridge-published collection showing how deeply Jesus is woven into Islamic devotional literature.
- **How Jesus Became God** — Bart D. Ehrman. An academic (non-Muslim, non-confessional) historian's account of how beliefs about Jesus' divinity developed in the earliest centuries.
- **Trinity (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry)** — Dale Tuggy.
- **Mere Christianity** — C.S. Lewis. A classic popular presentation of the mainstream Christian case, included so readers can hear that position from one of its best-known advocates.
- **Muslim-Christian Encounters: Perceptions and Misperceptions** — W. Montgomery Watt. A respected Western scholar of Islam on how the two faiths have understood and misunderstood each other.

quranVerses.arabic: يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لَا تَغْلُوا۟ فِى دِينِكُمْ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلْحَقَّ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ وَكَلِمَتُهُۥٓ أَلْقَىٰهَآ إِلَىٰ مَرْيَمَ وَرُوحٌۭ مِّنْهُ ۖ فَـَٔامِنُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَرُسُلِهِۦ ۖ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ ثَلَٰثَةٌ ۚ ٱنتَهُوا۟ خَيْرًۭا لَّكُمْ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱللَّهُ إِلَٰهٌۭ وَٰحِدٌۭ ۖ سُبْحَٰنَهُۥٓ أَن يَكُونَ لَهُۥ وَلَدٌۭ ۘ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۗ وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ وَكِيلًۭا
quranVerses.translation: O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion or say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary and a soul [created at a command] from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And do not say, "Three"; desist - it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.

faq.question: Do Muslims believe in Jesus?
faq.answer: Yes — belief in Jesus is mandatory in Islam. Muslims believe he is the Messiah, born of the Virgin Mary, a mighty messenger of God who performed miracles by God's permission. Rejecting Jesus would place a person outside Islam.

faq.question: Do Muslims believe Jesus is God or the son of God?
faq.answer: No. The Quran teaches that Jesus is God's servant and messenger, fully human, and explicitly states that God is exalted above having a son (Quran 4:171). Islam sees the deification of Jesus as the kind of 'excess in religion' the Quran warns against.

faq.question: Does Islam accept the virgin birth of Jesus?
faq.answer: Yes. The Quran narrates the annunciation to Mary and her astonished question — 'How will I have a child when no man has touched me?' — answered by God's creative command: 'Be,' and it is (Quran 3:47). The virgin birth is a miracle of creation, not proof of divine sonship.

faq.question: What does 'Messiah' mean in Islam?
faq.answer: Al-Masih (the Messiah) is a title of honor the Quran gives uniquely to Jesus, marking him as the anointed one promised to the Children of Israel. The Quran pairs the title with 'son of Mary' and 'messenger of Allah' (Quran 4:171, 5:75), so in Islam it does not imply divinity.

faq.question: Do Muslims believe Jesus was crucified?
faq.answer: Mainstream Islamic teaching holds that Jesus was not killed by crucifixion but that God saved him and raised him to Himself, and that he will return before the end of time.

faq.question: If both faiths love Jesus, why does the difference matter?
faq.answer: Because both faiths agree that who God is — and who may be worshiped — is the most important question a person faces. If Jesus is God, refusing him worship is a grave error; if he is God's human messenger, directing worship to him is exactly the excess the Quran, and arguably Jesus' own recorded words, warn against.
